Subject: Dedicated capacity — throughput / queueing behavior and exception request

Hi Olga,

We're finalizing the load test plan for BrightGrid's June launch. A couple of items on the Dedicated capacity SLA and reserved GPUs that we need clarified before we sign:

- Can you confirm per-GPU sustained throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) for the recommended model (redwood-large-enc)?
- How does Redwood handle queueing when reserved capacity hits 100%? Do requests queue at the customer lane, or do you have a global backpressure/priority queue?
- For a two-hour load window (planned June 15), we need a written commitment around latency (p95) and guaranteed reserved capacity for that window. If you can't hit the target, we'd like to understand variance / exception options and what the escalation/fallback looks like.

Attached is a draft SLA redline we're circulating internally — it's not final, but it lists our target: p95 < 250ms for user-facing text-generation endpoints during the window, and dedicated GPUs pinned to our account for the two hours.

Can you point us to the right person internally to approve a temporary SLA variance if needed? We're trying to avoid over-provisioning for the month but will pay for a short-term burst if you can support it.

Thanks,
Jane
Director, Platform Integrations
BrightGrid Energy

Hi Jane — thanks for the note and the redline.

Quick answers up front: we'll scope the exact tokens/sec with Marcus, and yes — we offer a short-term "burst" model on Dedicated that pins additional reserved GPUs for a defined window. Queueing behavior depends on how you configure prioritized lanes; by default requests for a Dedicated pool are backpressured into a per-customer queue with a configurable max depth, but we can provision a non-queued priority lane for critical endpoints.

To proceed: could you share the target request shape (QPS per endpoint, avg tokens, peak concurrency) for the June 15 window? If you can provide that by EOD Thursday we'll run a capacity plan and propose a written variance (addendum) with explicit metrics and escalation steps.

Looping in Marcus (SE) to provide the throughput/queueing notes and Stephanie for contracts/finance so we can scope pricing for the temporary capacity.

—Olga

Hi Jane / Olga,

I've run a rough sizing estimate based on the redwood-large-enc profile and historical throughput for similar workloads. A few important notes:

- Baseline: one rGPU (A100-equivalent) running segmented quantized redwood-large-enc can sustain ~110–140 text-generation requests/sec for short sequences (<=128 tokens) with KV-cache reuse. For longer sequences (~512 tokens) expect sustained ~25–40 requests/sec.
- Queueing: Dedicated pools maintain a per-customer FIFO queue that accepts up to a configurable queue_depth parameter; when queue is full we return 429s unless you opt-in for priority lane behavior. Priority lanes reserve N GPUs that are never queue-backed (requests either execute immediately or are rejected when capacity is consumed).
- Burst model: we can temporarily attach N extra reserved GPUs to your pool for a fixed window. That capacity is treated as Dedicated for the window (no routing to other customers).
- Fallbacks: we support automatic model-variant fallback (smaller quantized model) or region fallback if latency SLO is at risk; both are opt-ins and require pre-approval due to impact on fidelity.

Attached is a short CSV with measured queueing latency vs queue_depth for similar configs. If you want p95 < 250ms for a two-hour window with avg 200 concurrent short requests (<=128 tokens), my estimate is a reserved pool of ~30–40 GPUs with a priority lane for your critical endpoints. If you can confirm exact request sizes / concurrency I can tighten that.

—Marcus
Marcus Lin
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Marcus — that helps.

Confirming our test profile: 2 endpoints, each ~120 tokens avg, combined peak concurrency 220 requests, 90% short (<128) profile. Our target is: during the two-hour load window (June 15 local time) we must have p95 latency < 250ms for both endpoints. We agree to pay for burst; we're asking that Redwood commit, in writing, to the latency target and to pin the reserved GPUs (no preemptions) for the window.

Please treat this as a formal request for a temporary SLA variance/addendum: attach to the final MSA a one-time exception that documents the metrics, the GPU count for the window, monitoring/alerting thresholds, and the rollback/escalation steps if SLOs are missed. We will need legal/finance signatures; I've attached our redline for convenience (BrightGrid_SLA_Redline_v3.pdf).

Let me know what you need from Redwood's side to produce a draft addendum.

Jane

Approved with conditions.

I agree we should support BrightGrid's June 15 window with a timeboxed operational exception, subject to the following:
1) One-time premium for burst capacity — charge 1.5x standard reserved GPU rate for the two-hour window (include minimum guarantee of 30 GPUs). If they need >30, price incremental GPUs at 1.2x.
2) Ops constraint — Marcus to produce a capacity plan and run a smoke test with our staging region by June 10. No variance will be granted until the smoke test passes.
3) Legal addendum — Stephanie, please draft a short addendum with concrete metrics (p95 < 250ms), monitoring/alerting, rollback steps, and a remediations/credits clause limited to the window. Legal should sign-off before sending to customer.
4) No permanent SLA change — this is an explicit one-off exception; do not update standard MSA SLA language.

Olga — please confirm you'll communicate the terms to Jane and get a formal acceptance. Marcus / Stephanie: coordinate on the plan and the draft addendum. Once legal signs, we'll approve the signature.

—Vivek
